to arrange, line up

meervoud van het zelfstandig naamwoord opstel

forms.form:

glosses: op zijn plaats zetten

examples.text: De camera's waren al opgesteld.
In het Palais des Bonbons et du Nougat in Montélimar is met klassieke auto's een file opgesteld. In Pouilly-sur-Loire staat Les 200 Bornes, een pompstation annex hotel-restaurant in oude stijl.
Eindeloos veel tentjes stonden verdekt opgesteld onder de laaghangende boomtakken.

glosses: op schrift zetten

examples.text: Het contract werd daarna snel opgesteld.

glosses: ontwerpen

examples.text: 'Goed, dan stellen wij wel een schema op, hè, Olive?' Olive stak haar kin naar voren.

glosses: zich een bepaalde houding aanmeten

examples.text: Ik werd er ook minder dominant van, ik moest me flexibel opstellen, kreeg niet altijd mijn zin en had meer aandacht voor andere mensen die binnen groepen ook weinig zeiden.

glosses: To ready for use.

examples.text: We set up the sprinkler.

glosses: To arrange logically.

examples.text: Set up my CD collection.

glosses: To cause to happen.

examples.text: Even a minor change can set up new bugs.
England's famous victory sets up a meeting with Sweden in Samara on Saturday

glosses: To trap or ensnare.

examples.text: I've got to set up that tasty rabbit.

glosses: To arrange for an outcome; to tamper or rig.

examples.text: The election was set up!

glosses: To ready something for use.
To gel or harden.

examples.text: Give the cement 24 hours to set up before walking on it.

glosses: To level to rise in one part of a body of water, especially a shallow one, because of a storm surge caused by persistent wind.

examples.text: The level set up at the south end of the lake after a day of north winds.

glosses: To provide the money or other support that someone needs for an important task or activity.

examples.text: Winning the lottery has set them up for life.
A good breakfast really sets you up for the day.
If you ever need anything, come back here, and I'll set you up!

glosses: To establish someone in a business or position.

examples.text: She set herself up as an interior designer.
After he left college, his father set him up in the family business.

glosses: To trick or lure (someone) in order to entrap them.

examples.text: They claimed that they weren't selling drugs, but that they'd been set up by the police.

glosses: To make (someone) proud or conceited (often in passive).

examples.text: M. Robespierre looked at me sideways and smiled and said to Madame, ‘You're a young lady after my own heart.’ This set her up for the day.

glosses: To matchmake; to arrange a date between two people.
To create a goalscoring opportunity (for).

examples.text: Just past the hour Agbonlahor set up the second, crossing for Bent to net.
On 71.05, Portu brilliantly set up Yangel Herrera, only for Marc-André ter Stegen to make a sensational save.

glosses: To begin business or a scheme of life.

examples.text: to set up in trade; to set up for oneself

glosses: To profess openly; to make pretensions.

examples.text:
1744 (first printed) Jonathan Swift, On the Testimony of Conscience
those men who set up for morality without regard to religion, are generally virtuous but in part

glosses: To found; to start (a business, scheme)

examples.text: With the help of his wife Bilquis, he set up a maternal health clinic and a centre for abandoned children.

glosses: To deceive an opponent and capitalize on their reactions with a certain technique or maneuver.

examples.text: When you make an opening you merely cause an opponent to uncover a target somewhere on his person. But when you set up an opponent, you knock him off balance with one punch so that he should be an open target for a following punch. Unless he's knocked off balance, he's not set up.

Writer Danny Wamboldt of Ring magazine said, "Only Willie knew how to set up his opponents masterfully and then move in." Wamboldt, a former New England bantamweight champion and current national president of the Veteran Boxers Association, said that one of Pep's opponents said of his dazzling speed: "It was the first time he had been surrounded by one man."

glosses: To cause to take flight; to flush into the air.

examples.text: Edmund had enjoyed a good gallop over the downs, setting up the sandpipers[.]

glosses: Synonym of compose (To arrange (types) in a composing stick for printing; to typeset)
In a position to function; ready.

examples.text: Now that I'm set up, this will take moments!

glosses: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see write, down.

examples.text: I can't write down in the basement; it's cold there and my fingers cramp and get stiff.

glosses: To produce or set (something) down in writing; to record something.
To write (something) in a simple or condescending style.

examples.text: Good heavens, I can't write down to the level of the vulgar public!

glosses: To make a downward adjustment in the value of an asset.
To condemn in writing; to document the faults, offenses, or wrongdoing of.

examples.text: By 1859, D. Morier Evans was exhibiting [George] Hudson as the principal character in his rogues' gallery entitled "Facts, Failures and Frauds"; and at the hands of modern economic historians he has been written down as a common swindler.
See also: cite

glosses: An item of information put into a temporary or permanent physical medium.

examples.text: The person had a record of the interview so she could review her notes.
The tourist's photographs and the tape of the police call provide a record of the crime.
He draws eclectically on studies of baboons, descriptive anthropological accounts of hunter-gatherer societies and, in a few cases, the fossil record.

glosses: Any instance of a physical medium on which information was put for the purpose of preserving it and making it available for future reference.

examples.text: We have no record of you making this payment to us.

glosses: Ellipsis of phonograph record (“a disc, usually made from vinyl, on which sound is recorded and may be replayed on a phonograph”).

examples.text: I still like records better than CDs.
He's the record doctor / Tell him your woes / He'll reach in his bag / And he'll give you a dose

glosses: A set of data relating to a single individual or item.

examples.text: Pull up the record on John Smith. What's his medical history?

glosses: A data structure similar to a struct, in some programming languages such as C and Java based on classes and designed for storing immutable data.

examples.text: This chapter examines another data structure, the record (available in Pascal but not in all other high-level languages). Records make it easier to organize and represent information in Pascal, a major reason for the popularity of the Pascal[…]
The new record type provides another solution. A record is a class-like construct for data classes, a restricted form of class like enums and annotations.
A record is a special kind of class that's designed to work well with immutable (readonly) data.

glosses: The most extreme known value of some variable, particularly that of an achievement in competitive events.

examples.text: The heat and humidity were both new records.
Australia set a record of 10 back-to-back T20I wins.
He broke the record for the youngest English captain.
The team set a new record for most points scored in a game.

"Avanti has literally broken records over the last six months for delays and cancellations, and the Conservatives' answer is to reward failure with millions more in taxpayer cash," said Labour Shadow Transport Secretary Louise Haigh.

glosses: Enough to break previous records and set a new one; world-class; historic.

examples.text: "But it's far worse for me," said Edmund, "because you'll at least have a room of your own and I shall have to share a bedroom with that record stinker, Eustace."

glosses: To make a record of information.

examples.text: I wanted to record every detail of what happened, for the benefit of future generations.

The display and result must be placed in the context that was it was against a side that looked every bit their Fifa world ranking of 141 - but England completed the job with efficiency to record their biggest away win in 19 years.

glosses: To make an audio or video recording of.

examples.text: Within a week they had recorded both the song and the video for it.
However, the ability to record people without their knowledge, with the stroke of a finger over the spectacle frame or a voice command, has prompted privacy concerns.

glosses: To give legal status to by making an official public record.

examples.text: When the deed was recorded, we officially owned the house.

glosses: To fix in a medium, usually in a tangible medium.
To make an audio, video, or multimedia recording.
To repeat; to practice.
To sing or repeat a tune.

examples.text:
1595, George Peele, The Old Wives’ Tale, The Malone Society Reprints, 1908, lines 741-742,
Come Berecynthia, let vs in likewise,
And heare the Nightingale record hir notes.

They long’d to see the day, to heare the larke
Record her hymnes and chant her carols blest,

[…] the Nymph did earnestly contest
Whether the Birds or she recorded best […]

glosses: To reflect; to ponder.

examples.text: […] he was […] carried to the Scaffold on the Tower-hill […], himself praying all the way, and recording upon the words which he before had read.

glosses: Rédiger, libeller, élaborer, dresser.

examples.text: Een artikel opstellen.
Een proces-verbaal opstellen.

glosses: Placer, ranger, installer, monter, mettre en place, incorporer, encastrer, loger.

examples.text: Zodra de apparatuur perfect was opgesteld.
examples.translation: Dès que le matériel fut en exacte ordonnance.

examples.text: Zich opstellen.
examples.translation: Prendre une position, adopter un point de vue.
